links.reason: 83 opens இனையன நினைவுறீஇ, so the crowning follows the sight of the white hair, but that is story order. Neither verse says anything about a teacher's absence; the teaches claim is an inference from silence.

1051 puts the blame on the worthy giver who withholds (கரப்பின் அவர்பழி). 384's giver hides what he has out of pity (பெறாஅன் பேதுறுதல் எண்ணிப் பொறாஅன் கரந்து) and the proverb blames numbers (பன்மையோ தீது), a real limit on the rule.

1435's monkey (நோய்முதிர் குரங்கு) is a simile for a man gazing at pleasure; 2721's monkeys are a scene of a tryst. The shared word is குரங்கு/மந்தி, and the teaches (the lesson reaches the king as sight) is not in either verse; 2721 is also flagged uncertain.

1224 says the kings, knowing ruin awaits (உணர்ந்தும்), still keep மானம், which touches 969's மானம் வரின் உயிர்நீப்பர். But the teaches relies on a war 'already decided' and an unjust demand that the verse does not state; the pairing is mostly shared topic.

The note says Kattiyangaran took the land by a false gift (வஞ்சம்), but 240 says நீதியால் நிலம் கொண்ட, lawfully, and வஞ்சம் is not in the verse. Only the seizing of his goods answers the usurper; the 'fraud closed' framing is not in the Tamil.

Both are prophecies in different epics, but 105 reports a sage's saying with an uncertain line and no confirming scene, while 109 is the court's affirmation. The teaches (a later scene confirms the prophecy) does not hold for 105, and the pairing is only shared theme.
links.text_issue: 105 sense uncertain; கண்டிறந் துந்திடுங் காவலன் hard

links.reason: Both exclude those who do not reach/praise the Lord (இறைவன் அடிசேராதார்; நாவி னவிற்றாதார் வீட்டுலக நண்ணாரே). The Jina's attributes make the same exclusion concrete, but the epic-side gains clause is vague and the couplet does not name its Lord.

Two verses of one sermon: 2057 says right vision is easy for the great, 2067 states what right vision with tapas brings. The second does not turn the rarity into a promise; it closes the account of the four destinies, so this is adjacency.

260 lists among the king's killers வளை கய மடந்தை கொல்லும் and his own fault; 1813 has Vijayai say Saccandan died என்கட் டங்கிய அன்பினால். The woman's own words fulfil the earlier warning, a real prophecy-and-event pair, though the note selects from 260's list.

281 has the snake joining the sun's running disc (அரவு சேர்ந்து ஆங்கு ஓடு கதிர் வட்டம்); 290 has the minister, a great snake, swallowing the king-sun (கதிரினை ... மா நாகமுடன் விழுங்கிற்று). The same eclipse image is turned from a shield to the king.

This is story order: the portrait is carried (131) then shown (133). The teaches says the picture needs no word, but 131 sends the woman with a message (அறிவி) and 133 begins with the king lacking the man's word, so the portrait supplements speech.

The envoys name a stark choice (இரண்டிலொன் றுரைமின்), the opposite of 685's envoy who avoids the harsh (தூவாத நீக்கி). That is contrast, not a limit on the rule, and the teaches (the cost of the rule) and the war outcome are not in the verse.
Tivittan's roar at the cave is a scene of boldness, which illustrates அஞ்சாமை. Nothing in the verse shows its cost or a king's four qualities; the couplet gains only an example.

Both name the lute's parts (பத்தர்/பத்தல், ஆணி, மருப்பு, நரம்பு), a real lexical match. But the note says the epic lute has power over the hostile and wild, which 722 does not say (it sets out to hold the world in its sound), and borrowing is not shown.
1818 has the friends bow to Vijayai and leave; 1882 has them report finding her. That is plot order, and the teaches claim that he asks twice and the news is a report is not in these verses.

Tirumanthiram 533 makes dog births a result of wronging the mantra's teachers; 945 has the hero whisper the mantras to a dying dog. These are not incompatible claims about the same thing; they share the word dog. 945 also never says the dog becomes a god and has a corrupt line.
2722's rebuke (பரத்தையர்த் தோய்ந்த மார்பம்) follows the sight in 2721, but this is the next verse in the same scene. The teaches adds only that the mate's voice is heard.

274 uses lovely daughters only as a simile for a miser's wealth passing to a stranger. 228 says a girl is a jewel past counting and says nothing about her being given away, so the teaches (a king's weightiest care is her giving) is not in the Tamil.

290 asks the king to give the warrior toddy first (இவற்கு ஈந்து உண்மதி), and 298's warrior complains of dregs and not being sent first (நீ முந்து). The shared toddy and vanguard motif is real, but neither limits the other, so same_image fits better.

2463 only sets out the altar and bowls and makes no claim about the rite. Siddhar 372 condemns the show of practitioners (இவர் செய்யும்), and its marker says it may not condemn the rites themselves. There is no incompatible claim.

123 describes a king's desire as a sea with the breast as raft; Naladiyar 17 warns that a spear-eyed woman will stoop with a staff. They are not the same woman and no claim conflicts. The note's pay-with-his-land is not in 123.

The spear-eyed bride (வேனிரைச்செய் கண்ணி) matches the uncle's daughter with spear-like eyes in 26, and the patikam does promise the marriage. But the shaving and bathing the teaches mentions are not in 2490 and the uncle's daughter is not named in it.

183 has the lowest of the four orders learn and the highest come to him (கீழ்ப்பால் ஒருவன் கற்பின் மேற்பால் ஒருவனும் அவன்கண் படுமே); 409 keeps மேற்பிறந்தார்/கீழ்ப்பிறந்தும் while ranking learning above them. Both keep the orders as the thing learning overturns, and the cross-book pairing shows that.

2722's honey and neem mark a wife's refusal of a man who has lain with courtesans; Tirumanthiram 207 says women's sweetness turns to neem in the body. The shared bitter neem is a stock pair, and the epic verse is not an ascetic's verdict on pleasure as the gains clause says.

144 follows 143 (the hero enjoys Ilakkanai, sages arrive, he asks). That is sequence; the teaches that the poem puts pleasure under teaching is the grader's inference, not a limit stated by either verse.

Both say a king gripped by desire fails, but 251's maxim is about lacking learned men, while 9 has the king refuse counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்). It is a cross-epic parallel, not one developing the other.

Gunamalai's threat of death or penance (இறத்தல் ஒன்றோ ... தவம்) shows fixed constancy before marriage, which Kural 54 praises in a wife as திண்மை. The extension is real but modest, and the epic-side gains clause is an imposed reading.

409 has the astrologer assert the omen; 639 has Acuvakanthan ask a conditional question about the omen-book being a deceit (பொச்சலாங்கொல்). That is not an incompatible claim, and the two verses belong to different courts.

3101 praises the Lord's feet as a spear cutting karma (கருவினை துணிக்கும் எஃகமே); Tirumanthiram 219 has the worshipped fire burn deeds (வினைசுடு). Both say worship removes karma, which is parallel, not incompatible. That the Jina does not answer prayer is not in the verse.
294 is a bare list of queens with no verb; the Naladiyar warning is brought in from the next kandam, which the verse does not show. The note itself says the verse never voices it.

Both break the body into blood, skin and fat to undo desire (நெய்த்தோர்... தோல்; குருதியும் என்பும்... தோலும்). The shared list is real, but the gains clauses are vague, and the addressees (his wives) are from the marker, not stated in the verse.
Both compare the city to wish-trees (கற்பகம்), but that is a stock image of plenty and 2404 lists festival goods in incense smoke. The teaches (the image follows the occasion) is thin.

352 praises a bard's tune on Anji (அஞ்சி நல்லிசை நிறுத்த... பனுவல்), and Purananuru 92 is Avvai's song to Anji, but 352 does not name Avvai or say it is that song. The link rests on the name Anji plus an inference the Tamil does not fix.

1720 has the three orders praise those who bore the child (ஈண்டிச் செல்வனைப் பொறுத்தவர் பொலிவுரை); 70 makes the same praise the son's gift (என்நோற்றான் கொல்). The timing contrast is real but thin; the couplet's own gains are a stretch.

799 warns the dying to avoid evil in the body they will next take (இனிக்கொள்ளும் உடம்பினும்); Tirumanthiram 2133 describes the subtle body taking a new body. Rebirth is shared, but the claim that the Jain verse 'presupposes' Tirumular's mechanism crosses schools.

72 reverses 68's stripping by the prince's winnings and gifts, which is a real reversal but not an incompatible claim, so develops fits. 72 gives the kings their own goods back and the rest to his mother; being richer in standing is not stated.
2823's seed-in-good-soil teaching is clear, but 2622 is tangled (the note's 'never give a handful' is a construal). The pairing as the teacher answering Vijayai is the grader's reconstruction.

1666 line 4 (வேண்டிய விளைத்துக் கொள்ளும் விழுத்தவம்) restates 265's வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங் கெய்தலால், so it agrees rather than limits. The prank motive is not in the verse, which has only a trembling woman and the king's reassurance.
Both call the body a worm-filled filth (புழுமொய்ப்ப; புழுக்கூடு), a stock image. The gains claims do not hold: a Jain teacher's verse does not gain Siva's feet, and the teaches is the shared theme.
1019 has Kaman take aim; 1021 has desire grow. The teaches (the lover himself feeds it) depends on reading வில்வலான் as the youth, but it may be Kaman. That is a reading-dependent plot step.

146 does say the king dwells with desire burning (காமம் உள் சுட); 233 blames bathing in the liquor of lust (காமம் என்னும் மதுவினில்). But the pavilion is not the liquor, and the note's minister is a personified wisdom (அறிவு).

1648 அழலிற் சாராது அகலாது ஒழுக is the fire-warming rule of 691, applied to pupils. That is real, but the 'hidden king' teaches is plot knowledge outside the verse, and 691 concerns quarrelsome kings (இகல் வேந்தர்).

13 says she resolved to look on no male form (ஆண் உரு யாதும் நோக்காள்); 899 gives the vow with its condition, his coming defeated to worship her feet (தோற்று வந்து என் சிலம்படி கைதொழ). The scene sharpens the patikam summary. The reading of நோற்பன் is hard.
